topics.title: Angles as rotation: degrees and radians

learn.hook: A ceiling fan blade, a Ferris wheel at a Dussehra mela and the hands of a clock all sweep angles far bigger than 90° — so trigonometry must grow up beyond right triangles.
points: In Class 10, trigonometric ratios were defined for acute angles. Now we extend them to angles of any size, and then to any real number.
An angle is the amount of rotation of a ray from its initial side to its terminal side. Anticlockwise rotation gives a positive angle; clockwise gives a negative one.
Degree measure: one full turn = 360°; 1° = 60′ (minutes), 1′ = 60″ (seconds).
Radian measure: the angle at the centre subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius is 1 radian. In general θ = l/r (θ in radians).
Convention: when no unit is written, the angle is in radians. So 'sin 2' means the sine of 2 radians, and θ = π/3 means π/3 radians.

example.q: An arc of length 18 cm subtends an angle θ at the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm. Find θ.
steps: Use θ = l/r with l = 18 cm and r = 6 cm.

learn.reallife: An ISRO antenna turning 'through 2 radians' and a cricket ball spinning several full turns both use rotation measure that can exceed 360°.

games.title: Angle basics
items: An angle can be greater than 360°.
More than one full rotation is allowed, e.g. 450°.
A clockwise rotation gives a positive angle.
By convention anticlockwise is positive, clockwise is negative.
θ = l/r gives θ in degrees.
θ = l/r gives the angle in radians.
If an angle is written without units, it is taken in radians.
Degrees split into minutes, minutes into seconds.
1 radian is the angle of an arc equal to the diameter.
It is the angle of an arc equal to the radius.

quiz.q: An arc of length 12 cm subtends an angle of 1.5 radians at the centre. What is the radius?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies l by θ instead of dividing

quiz.q: A circle has radius 10 cm. What arc length subtends an angle of 2.5 radians?
quiz.mistake: Divides r by θ

quiz.q: How many seconds (″) are there in 1°?
quiz.mistake: Stops at 60 minutes

quiz.q: A ray rotates three-quarters of a full turn clockwise. The angle formed is:
quiz.explain: Three-quarters of 360° is 270°; clockwise makes it negative.
steps: Clockwise rotation gives a negative angle
quiz.mistake: Ignores the direction of rotation

quiz.q: In the statement 'sin 1 > 0', the angle 1 is measured in:
quiz.explain: Angles written without units are radians by convention.
steps: Convention: when no unit is written, the angle is in radians
The angle is measured in radians
quiz.mistake: Assumes degrees whenever no unit is shown

quiz.q: Which angle is the same as 1 full revolution plus a quarter turn anticlockwise?
quiz.explain: 360° + 90° = 450°, positive because anticlockwise.
steps: Anticlockwise, so the angle is positive
quiz.mistake: Forgets the full revolution

quiz.q: Why do we need trigonometric functions of angles larger than 90°?
options: Rotations such as wheels and clock hands go beyond a right angle, and right-triangle ratios only cover acute angles
Acute angles do not have trigonometric ratios
Radians only work for obtuse angles
quiz.explain: Right triangles only give ratios for 0° < θ < 90°. Defining functions for any angle lets us describe all rotations and periodic motion.
steps: Right-triangle ratios only work for acute angles, 0° < θ < 90°
Wheels and clock hands keep rotating far beyond 90°
To describe all rotations we need trig functions for any angle
So: rotations go beyond a right angle, and right-triangle ratios only cover acute angles
Answer: Rotations such as wheels and clock hands go beyond a right angle, and right-triangle ratios only cover acute angles
quiz.mistake: Thinks trigonometry is only about triangles

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An angle of 2 radians is larger than a right angle.
Reason (R): 1 radian is about 57°16′.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: 2 radians ≈ 114°32′, which is more than 90°. R gives the size of 1 radian, which explains A.
steps: A follows directly from the size of 1 radian in R
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats 2 radians as 2°

teach.ask: Gappu says 'angles are just triangles' corners, between 0° and 90°'. Explain angles as rotation, and what a radian is.
teach.praise: So a radian is an arc as long as the radius, and angles can keep spinning past 360°!
teach.nudge: What exactly is 1 radian — which length equals which?

revise.summary: An angle measures the rotation of a ray from its initial to its terminal side: anticlockwise is positive, clockwise negative. It is measured in degrees (360° per turn) or radians, where θ = l/r.
focus: Give the sign of an angle from the direction of rotation
Use θ = l/r (θ in radians) to find an angle or an arc length
Convert between degrees, minutes and seconds
Read angles with no unit as radians
remember: Anticlockwise rotation: positive angle; clockwise: negative angle
1 radian: angle subtended at the centre by an arc equal to the radius; θ = l/r
No unit written → the angle is in radians
traps: Don't read 'sin 2' as sin 2°: it means 2 radians
Don't use θ in degrees in l = rθ

topics.title: Converting degrees and radians; arc problems

learn.hook: A Ferris wheel turning 540 times a minute? That's a centrifuge! Converting revolutions, degrees and radians is daily work for engineers.
points: A full circle is 2π radians = 360°, so π radians = 180°.
Degrees → radians: multiply by π/180. Radians → degrees: multiply by 180/π.
1 radian = 180°/π ≈ 57°16′ (approx.) and 1° = π/180 ≈ 0.01746 radian (approx.).
For degree–minute form, first change minutes to degrees: 47°30′ = 47.5° = 95/2 degrees.
Arc problems use l = rθ (θ in radians). One revolution = 2π radians; when a number is needed, NCERT often uses π = 22/7.
learn.reallife: A Mumbai local's wheel of radius 0.5 m that turns through 2π radians moves the train 2π × 0.5 ≈ 3.14 m — arc length is distance travelled.

quiz.q: A wheel makes 360 revolutions in one minute. Through how many radians does it turn in one second?
quiz.explain: 360 rev/min = 6 rev/s. Each revolution is 2π, so 6 × 2π = 12π radians.
steps: 360 revolutions per minute ÷ 60 = 6 revolutions per second
The wheel turns 12π radians in one second
quiz.mistake: Forgets to convert minutes to seconds, or uses π per revolution

quiz.q: Convert 5π/3 radians to degrees.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by π/180 instead of 180/π

quiz.q: A pendulum 60 cm long swings so that its tip moves along an arc of 15 cm. The angle of swing in radians is:
quiz.explain: θ = l/r = 15/60 = 1/4 radian.
steps: Given: r = 60 cm, arc l = 15 cm
quiz.mistake: Divides r by l

quiz.q: Find the length of the minor arc of a circle of radius 21 cm cut off by a chord equal to the radius. (Use π = 22/7.)
quiz.explain: A chord equal to the radius makes an equilateral triangle, so the angle is 60° = π/3. Arc = 21 × π/3 = 7π = 22 cm.
quiz.mistake: Takes the arc as equal to the chord

quiz.q: Arcs of the same length in two circles subtend 45° and 60° at their centres. Find the ratio r₁ : r₂.
quiz.explain: l = r₁(π/4) = r₂(π/3) gives r₁/r₂ = (π/3)/(π/4) = 4/3.
steps: Same arc l in both circles: l = r₁θ₁ = r₂θ₂
quiz.mistake: Thinks bigger angle means bigger radius

quiz.q: Convert 40°20′ to radians.
Using π = 22/7, convert 11/16 radian to degrees.
quiz.mistake: Stops at decimal minutes or rounds too early

quiz.q: The minute hand of a clock is 1.5 cm long. How far does its tip move in 40 minutes? (Use π = 3.14.)
quiz.explain: In 40 minutes the hand turns 40/60 × 360° = 240° = 4π/3. Distance = 1.5 × 4π/3 = 2π = 6.28 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses 40° instead of 240°

teach.ask: Gappu needs to change 135° to radians and back. Explain the rule connecting degrees and radians and how to find an arc length.
teach.praise: π radians = 180°, and arc = radius × angle. Converting is a breeze now!
teach.nudge: What is π radians equal to in degrees?

revise.summary: Since π radians = 180°, multiply by π/180 to change degrees to radians and by 180/π to change radians to degrees. Arc problems use l = rθ with θ in radians.
focus: Convert degrees (including minutes) to radians and radians to degrees
Solve arc, pendulum and wheel problems with l = rθ
Turn revolutions into radians using 1 revolution = 2π
remember: π radians = 180°; 2π radians = 360°
Degrees → radians: × π/180; radians → degrees: × 180/π
traps: Change minutes to degrees before converting: 47°30′ = 47.5°, not 47.30°
Don't forget that one revolution is 2π radians, not π

topics.title: Trigonometric functions on the unit circle

learn.hook: Watch a point riding a circle of radius 1 — its x-coordinate is cos x and its y-coordinate is sin x. Every trig fact follows from that one picture.
points: Take the unit circle centred at O. If the arc from (1, 0) to P has length x (radians), then P = (cos x, sin x). Since P is on the circle, cos²x + sin²x = 1.
tan x = sin x/cos x (cos x ≠ 0), cot x = cos x/sin x (sin x ≠ 0), sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x.
Quadrantal values: sin 0 = 0, sin π/2 = 1, sin π = 0, sin 3π/2 = −1, sin 2π = 0; cos 0 = 1, cos π/2 = 0, cos π = −1, cos 3π/2 = 0, cos 2π = 1.
sin x = 0 exactly when x = nπ; cos x = 0 exactly when x = (2n + 1)π/2, where n is any integer.
Dividing cos²x + sin²x = 1 by cos²x or sin²x: 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x.

example.q: Find the value of sin²(π/4) + cos²(π/6) − tan²(π/3).

learn.reallife: Sound engineers at AIR model a pure tone as y = sin(ωt): the up-and-down motion of a point going round a circle.

quiz.q: What is the value of sin(3π/2) + cos(π)?
quiz.explain: sin(3π/2) = −1 and cos π = −1, so the sum is −2.
steps: cos π = −1 (left end of the circle)
quiz.mistake: Takes sin(3π/2) as +1

quiz.q: On the unit circle, the point reached after an arc of length x from (1, 0) is:
quiz.explain: The x-coordinate is cos x and the y-coordinate is sin x.
steps: On the unit circle, a point is (x-coordinate, y-coordinate)
The x-coordinate is cos x and the y-coordinate is sin x
So the point is (cos x, sin x)
quiz.mistake: Swaps sine and cosine

quiz.q: Find 2 cos²(π/4) + cosec²(7π/6) sin²(π/6).
quiz.explain: cos(π/4) = 1/√2 gives 2 × 1/2 = 1. cosec(7π/6) = −2 so cosec² = 4; sin²(π/6) = 1/4, product 1. Total 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes cosec(7π/6) = −1/2

quiz.q: For which values of x is cos x = 0?
quiz.explain: cos x is the x-coordinate, which is 0 at the top and bottom of the unit circle: odd multiples of π/2.
steps: cos x is the x-coordinate of the point on the unit circle
x-coordinate = 0 at the top (π/2) and bottom (3π/2), and every π after that
These are the odd multiples of π/2
cos x = 0 at x = (2n + 1)π/2, n ∈ Z
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the zeros of sin and cos

quiz.q: If sec x = 13/12, what is tan²x?
steps: Identity: 1 + tan²x = sec²x, so tan²x = sec²x − 1
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 instead of subtracting

quiz.q: tan x is NOT defined when:
quiz.explain: tan x = sin x/cos x, so it fails when cos x = 0, i.e. at odd multiples of π/2.
steps: A fraction is undefined when its denominator is 0
So tan x fails exactly when cos x = 0 (odd multiples of π/2)
tan x is not defined when cos x = 0
quiz.mistake: Confuses tan with cot

quiz.q: What is the value of cot²(π/4) + cosec(5π/6) + 3 tan²(π/3)?
quiz.mistake: Takes cosec(5π/6) as negative, getting 8

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): sin²x + cos²x = 1 for every real x.
Reason (R): (cos x, sin x) lies on the circle x² + y² = 1.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because P = (cos x, sin x) is on the unit circle, its coordinates satisfy x² + y² = 1. R explains A exactly.
steps: R: P = (cos x, sin x) lies on the unit circle x² + y² = 1, which is true
Substituting the coordinates: cos²x + sin²x = 1, which is A
So A is true, and it follows directly from R
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the identity only holds for acute angles

teach.ask: Gappu only knows sin as 'opposite over hypotenuse'. Explain how the unit circle defines sin x and cos x for every real x.
teach.praise: A point going round a circle: x is cos, y is sin. Simple and beautiful!
teach.nudge: On the unit circle, which coordinate gives cos x and which gives sin x?

revise.summary: On the unit circle, the point reached by an arc of length x from (1, 0) is (cos x, sin x), so cos²x + sin²x = 1. The other four functions are ratios or reciprocals of sin and cos.
focus: Read sin x and cos x as the coordinates of a point on the unit circle
Recall sin and cos at 0, π/2, π, 3π/2 and 2π
Find where sin x = 0, cos x = 0, and where tan, sec, cot and cosec are undefined
Use 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x
remember: P = (cos x, sin x) on the unit circle; cos²x + sin²x = 1
tan x = sin x/cos x, cot x = cos x/sin x, sec x = 1/cos x, cosec x = 1/sin x
sin x = 0 when x = nπ; cos x = 0 when x = (2n + 1)π/2
1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x
traps: The point is (cos x, sin x), not (sin x, cos x): cos is the x-coordinate
tan x is undefined where cos x = 0, not where sin x = 0

topics.title: Signs in the quadrants; finding all values from one

learn.hook: Know one trig value and the quadrant, and you can unlock all six — like knowing a locker code and the floor number.
points: Quadrant I (0 to π/2): all six functions positive.
Quadrant II (π/2 to π): only sin and cosec positive.
Quadrant III (π to 3π/2): only tan and cot positive.
Quadrant IV (3π/2 to 2π): only cos and sec positive.
Method: use sin²x + cos²x = 1 (or 1 + tan²x = sec²x) to find the size, then fix the sign from the quadrant.

example.q: If cos x = −12/13 and x lies in the third quadrant, find the other five trigonometric functions.
steps: In quadrant III, sin x < 0, so sin x = −5/13.
example.answer: sin x = −5/13, tan x = 5/12, cot x = 12/5, sec x = −13/12, cosec x = −13/5

learn.reallife: Navigators reading a compass bearing in the second quadrant know at once that the east–west component (cos) is negative — signs carry direction.

games.title: Sign check
items: 200° is in quadrant III, where sin is negative.
100° is in quadrant II, where cos is negative.
300° is in quadrant IV where cos, and hence sec, is positive.
150° is in quadrant II, where sin and cosec are positive.

quiz.q: If sin x = 3/5 and x lies in the second quadrant, then cos x is:
quiz.explain: cos²x = 1 − 9/25 = 16/25, and cos x < 0 in quadrant II, so cos x = −4/5.
steps: In quadrant II, cos x is negative
quiz.mistake: Keeps the positive square root regardless of quadrant

quiz.q: If tan x = −5/12 and x lies in the fourth quadrant, then sec x is:
quiz.explain: sec²x = 1 + 25/144 = 169/144. In quadrant IV cos x > 0, so sec x = 13/12.
steps: In quadrant IV, cos x > 0, so sec x > 0
quiz.mistake: Copies the negative sign of tan onto sec

quiz.q: If cot x = 3/4 and x lies in the third quadrant, then sin x is:
quiz.explain: cosec²x = 1 + 9/16 = 25/16, cosec x = −5/4 in quadrant III, so sin x = −4/5.
steps: In quadrant III, sin x < 0, so cosec x = −5/4
quiz.mistake: Picks the cosine value instead of sine

quiz.q: In which quadrant are both sin x and tan x negative?
quiz.explain: In quadrant IV, sin < 0 and cos > 0, so tan < 0 too. In II tan < 0 but sin > 0; in III tan > 0.
steps: Quadrant I: both positive; II: sin > 0, tan < 0
IV: sin < 0 and cos > 0, so tan = sin/cos < 0
Both negative in the fourth quadrant
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative sin always means quadrant III

quiz.q: If sec x = 13/5 and x lies in the fourth quadrant, then tan x is:
quiz.explain: tan²x = sec²x − 1 = 144/25, and tan < 0 in quadrant IV, so tan x = −12/5.
steps: In quadrant IV, tan x is negative
quiz.mistake: Forgets the sign rule for quadrant IV

quiz.q: If cos x = −1/2 and x lies in the third quadrant, then tan x is:
quiz.explain: sin x = −√3/2 in quadrant III, so tan x = (−√3/2)/(−1/2) = √3.
steps: sin²x = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4, so |sin x| = √3/2; in quadrant III sin x < 0 → sin x = −√3/2
quiz.mistake: Makes tan negative because cos is negative

quiz.q: If cosec x = −41/9 and x lies in the fourth quadrant, then cos x is:
quiz.explain: sin x = −9/41, cos²x = 1 − 81/1681 = 1600/1681, and cos > 0 in quadrant IV, so cos x = 40/41.
quiz.mistake: Uses the sign of cosec for cos

quiz.q: Which function is positive in quadrant III?
quiz.explain: In quadrant III, sin and cos are both negative, so their ratios tan and cot are positive.
steps: In quadrant III, sin x < 0 and cos x < 0
So sec x, cos x and sin x are all negative there
cot x is positive in quadrant III
quiz.mistake: Assumes everything is negative in quadrant III

teach.ask: Gappu knows cos x = −12/13 but can't decide whether sin x is +5/13 or −5/13. Explain how the quadrant decides the sign.
teach.praise: Use the identity for the size, the quadrant for the sign. Locker unlocked!
teach.nudge: Which quadrant are we in, and which functions are positive there?

revise.summary: The signs of the trig functions depend on the quadrant: all positive in I, only sin and cosec in II, only tan and cot in III, only cos and sec in IV. Find the size from an identity, then fix the sign.
focus: Recall which functions are positive in each quadrant
Find all six trig values from one value and the quadrant
Use sin²x + cos²x = 1, 1 + tan²x = sec²x and 1 + cot²x = cosec²x for the size
remember: Quadrant I: all positive; II: sin, cosec positive
Quadrant III: tan, cot positive; IV: cos, sec positive
Method: find the size from an identity, then choose the sign from the quadrant
traps: Don't drop the sign: the square root gives only the size
In quadrant III both sin and cos are negative, so tan and cot are positive

learn.hook: The monsoon returns every year, a pendulum every few seconds, and sin x every 2π. Periodicity lets you tame angles like 765° in one step.
points: sin and cos: domain R, range [−1, 1]. tan: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}, range R. cot: domain R − {nπ}, range R.
sec: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}; cosec: domain R − {nπ}. Both have range R − (−1, 1), i.e. |y| ≥ 1.
sin(2nπ + x) = sin x and cos(2nπ + x) = cos x: period 2π. tan(nπ + x) = tan x and cot(nπ + x) = cot x: period π.
Large angles: remove whole turns (multiples of 360° or 2π) first. sin 765° = sin(720° + 45°) = sin 45° = 1/√2.
Negative angles: cos(−x) = cos x and sin(−x) = −sin x. So cos(−1710°) = cos 1710° = cos(4 × 360° + 270°) = cos 270° = 0.
learn.reallife: The tides at Mumbai's coast follow an approximately periodic pattern, so planners model them with sine curves.

games.title: Match the function to its range
pairs: Range R; undefined at odd multiples of π/2
Range R; undefined at multiples of π

quiz.q: What is the value of tan(25π/3)?
quiz.explain: 25π/3 = 8π + π/3, and tan has period π, so tan(25π/3) = tan(π/3) = √3.
steps: tan has period π, so tan(8π + π/3) = tan(π/3)
quiz.mistake: Removes only 2π at a time and makes an arithmetic slip

quiz.q: What is sin(−17π/3)?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin(−x) = −sin x but then reduces 17π/3 wrongly

quiz.q: The range of cos x is:
quiz.explain: cos x is the x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle, so it lies between −1 and 1 inclusive.
steps: cos x is the x-coordinate of a point on the unit circle
So −1 ≤ cos x ≤ 1, with cos 0 = 1 and cos π = −1 reached
quiz.mistake: Thinks cos x is never negative

quiz.q: The domain of tan x is:
quiz.explain: tan x = sin x/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0, i.e. at odd multiples of π/2.
steps: tan x = sin x/cos x needs cos x ≠ 0
quiz.mistake: Uses the zeros of sin instead of cos

quiz.q: What is cot(−19π/4)?
quiz.explain: −19π/4 + 5π = π/4, and cot has period π, so the value is cot(π/4) = 1.
steps: cot has period π, so add 5π = 20π/4
quiz.mistake: Applies cot(−x) = −cot x without reducing, getting −1

quiz.q: Which value can sec x NEVER take?
quiz.explain: sec x = 1/cos x and |cos x| ≤ 1, so |sec x| ≥ 1. 1/2 is impossible.
steps: sec x = 1/cos x and −1 ≤ cos x ≤ 1
So |sec x| ≥ 1: sec x ≥ 1 or sec x ≤ −1
−3, 2 and −1 are allowed; 1/2 lies between −1 and 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks sec x has the same range as cos x

quiz.q: What is the period of tan x?
quiz.explain: tan(x + π) = tan x for all x in its domain, and no smaller positive number works.
steps: tan(x + π) = tan x for all x in the domain
No smaller positive number does this (π/2 makes tan undefined)
So the smallest repeat length is π
quiz.mistake: Assumes all trig functions have period 2π

quiz.q: Evaluate cos 1830°.
quiz.mistake: Reduces by 360° one time too many or too few

teach.ask: Gappu panics at 'sin 765°'. Explain what periodicity means and how to reduce big or negative angles.
teach.praise: 765° is just 45° after two full spins. Big angles don't scare me now!
teach.nudge: After how many degrees do sin and cos repeat their values?

revise.summary: sin and cos have domain R and range [−1, 1]; tan and sec exclude odd multiples of π/2, cot and cosec exclude multiples of π. sin and cos repeat every 2π, tan and cot every π.
focus: State the domain and range of all six trig functions
Reduce large angles by removing whole turns (360° or 2π)
Handle negative angles with cos(−x) = cos x and sin(−x) = −sin x
Use period π for tan and cot
remember: sin, cos: domain R, range [−1, 1]; tan: domain R − {(2n + 1)π/2}, range R
sec and cosec: range R − (−1, 1), i.e. |y| ≥ 1
Period of sin and cos: 2π; period of tan and cot: π
cos(−x) = cos x; sin(−x) = −sin x
traps: The range of cos x includes −1 and 1: it is [−1, 1], not (−1, 1)
sec x can never be a number between −1 and 1, such as 1/2

learn.hook: ECG waves at AIIMS, AC current in your home, and ocean waves — all look like the graph of sin x. Let's read those curves.
points: sin x: increases from 0 to 1 in quadrant I, decreases from 1 to 0 in II, decreases from 0 to −1 in III, increases from −1 to 0 in IV.
cos x: decreases from 1 to 0 in I and from 0 to −1 in II; increases from −1 to 0 in III and from 0 to 1 in IV.
tan x: increases in every quadrant — from 0 to ∞ in I, −∞ to 0 in II, 0 to ∞ in III and −∞ to 0 in IV — with vertical asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2.
Graphs of sin and cos are waves between −1 and 1 with period 2π; the cos graph is the sin graph shifted left by π/2.
cot has asymptotes at x = nπ; sec has asymptotes where cos x = 0 and cosec where sin x = 0, and their graphs never enter the band −1 < y < 1.

example.q: In which quadrants are both sin x and cos x decreasing?
steps: sin decreases in quadrants II and III.
cos decreases in quadrants I and II.
example.answer: Only in the second quadrant (π/2 < x < π)

learn.reallife: Household AC supply in India is 230 V at 50 Hz: the voltage traces a sine wave 50 times every second.

games.title: Match the graph feature
pairs: Asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2

quiz.q: In which quadrant does cos x increase from −1 to 0?
quiz.explain: At x = π, cos x = −1; at x = 3π/2, cos x = 0. That stretch is quadrant III.
steps: So cos x rises from −1 to 0 between π and 3π/2
quiz.mistake: Thinks cos only increases in quadrant I

quiz.q: The graph of y = sin x crosses the x-axis at:
quiz.explain: The zeros of sin x are exactly the integer multiples of π.
steps: y = sin x crosses the x-axis where sin x = 0
sin x = 0 exactly when x = nπ
(2n + 1)π/2 are the zeros of cos, not sin
quiz.mistake: Uses the zeros of cos x

quiz.q: Which is true about tan x in quadrant II?
quiz.explain: Just after π/2, tan x is a very large negative number, and it rises to 0 at π.
steps: Just after π/2, cos x is a tiny negative number and sin x ≈ 1, so tan x is a huge negative number
tan x increases in every quadrant
In quadrant II tan x increases from −∞ to 0
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative values must be decreasing

quiz.q: The maximum value of y = sin x is reached at:
quiz.explain: sin x = 1 at the top of the unit circle, x = π/2, and every 2π after that.
steps: sin x = 1 at the top of the unit circle, x = π/2
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the maximum of cos x at x = 0

quiz.q: Which graph has NO points with −1 < y < 1?
quiz.explain: |sec x| = 1/|cos x| ≥ 1, so the graph avoids that band. tan and cot take every real value.
steps: So |sec x| ≥ 1, and its graph never enters −1 < y < 1
sin x stays inside [−1, 1]; tan and cot take every real value
y = sec x has no points with −1 < y < 1
quiz.mistake: Thinks tan has the same range as sec

quiz.q: The graph of y = cos x can be obtained from y = sin x by:
options: shifting it π/2 to the left
shifting it π to the right
quiz.explain: cos x = sin(x + π/2), which is the sin graph moved left by π/2.
steps: Replacing x by x + π/2 moves a graph π/2 to the left
So the cos graph is the sin graph shifted left
Shift y = sin x by π/2 to the left
Answer: shifting it π/2 to the left
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong direction or a full π shift

quiz.q: How many times does the graph of y = sin x cut the x-axis for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
quiz.explain: It cuts at x = 0, π and 2π.
steps: y = sin x cuts the x-axis where sin x = 0, i.e. x = nπ
quiz.mistake: Leaves out one of the end points

quiz.q: Where does y = tan x have vertical asymptotes?
quiz.explain: tan x is undefined where cos x = 0, and the graph shoots off to ±∞ near those lines.
steps: tan x = sin x/cos x is undefined where cos x = 0
Near these lines the graph shoots to ±∞
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the asymptotes of tan and cot

teach.ask: Gappu is sketching y = sin x and y = tan x. Explain where each increases or decreases, and what the graphs look like.
teach.praise: A smooth wave for sin, a ladder of rising curves with walls for tan. Picture perfect!
teach.nudge: What happens to the graph of tan x near x = π/2?

revise.summary: sin and cos graphs are waves between −1 and 1 with period 2π, and cos is sin shifted left by π/2. tan increases in every quadrant with asymptotes at odd multiples of π/2; sec and cosec never enter −1 < y < 1.
focus: Describe how sin, cos and tan increase or decrease in each quadrant
Find zeros, maxima and asymptotes from the graphs
Relate the sin and cos graphs by a shift of π/2
remember: sin x: increases 0 → 1 in I, decreases 1 → 0 in II, 0 → −1 in III, increases −1 → 0 in IV
cos x: decreases 1 → 0 in I and 0 → −1 in II; increases −1 → 0 in III and 0 → 1 in IV
tan x increases in every quadrant; asymptotes at x = (2n + 1)π/2
cos x = sin(x + π/2): the sin graph shifted left by π/2
traps: sin x is zero at multiples of π, not at odd multiples of π/2
Don't forget both end points: sin x cuts the x-axis at 0, π and 2π on [0, 2π]

learn.hook: Every allied-angle trick — cos(π − x), sin(π/2 + x) — comes out of ONE formula: cos(x + y). Learn it once, and the rest follow.
points: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y. It is proved from the unit circle by equating the distance between two pairs of points on it.
Replace y by −y: cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.
cos(π/2 − x) = sin x, sin(π/2 − x) = cos x; cos(π/2 + x) = −sin x, sin(π/2 + x) = cos x.
cos(π − x) = −cos x, sin(π − x) = sin x; cos(π + x) = −cos x, sin(π + x) = −sin x.
cos(2π − x) = cos x, sin(2π − x) = −sin x.
learn.reallife: Phase-shift tricks such as cos(π/2 − x) = sin x are used in electrical engineering to compare AC voltages that are out of step.

games.title: Derive cos(x − y) from cos(x + y)
items: Start with cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y.
Use cos(−y) = cos y and sin(−y) = −sin y.
cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.

quiz.q: cos(x + y) equals:
options: cos x cos y + sin x sin y
sin x cos y + cos x sin y
cos x cos y − sin x sin y
quiz.explain: The sign between the terms is opposite to the sign inside: '+' inside gives '−' outside for cosine.
steps: For cosine, the sign between the terms is opposite to the sign inside
cos x + cos y is not a valid expansion; sin x cos y + cos x sin y is sin(x + y)
cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y
Answer: cos x cos y − sin x sin y
quiz.mistake: Uses the cos(x − y) sign

quiz.q: cos(π − x) equals:
quiz.explain: π − x is in quadrant II for acute x, where cos is negative. π is an even multiple of π/2, so the function stays cos: cos(π − x) = −cos x.
steps: For acute x, π − x lies in quadrant II, where cos is negative
π is an even multiple of π/2, so cos stays cos
quiz.mistake: Switches cos to sin for a π shift

quiz.q: Find the value of cos 70° cos 10° + sin 70° sin 10°.
quiz.explain: This is cos(70° − 10°) = cos 60° = 1/2.
steps: Pattern: cos A cos B + sin A sin B = cos(A − B)
quiz.mistake: Uses cos(70° + 10°) = cos 80°

quiz.q: sin(π/2 + x) equals:
quiz.explain: For acute x, π/2 + x is in quadrant II where sin is positive; π/2 changes sin to cos.
steps: For acute x, π/2 + x lies in quadrant II, where sin is positive
π/2 is an odd multiple of π/2, so sin changes to cos
quiz.mistake: Gives the sign of cos in quadrant II

quiz.q: What is cos 105°?
quiz.explain: cos(60° + 45°) = cos 60° cos 45° − sin 60° sin 45° = (1 − √3)/(2√2) = (√2 − √6)/4, a negative number as expected in quadrant II.
quiz.mistake: Uses the plus sign of cos(x − y)

quiz.q: Simplify sin(π/3 + x) cos x − cos(π/3 + x) sin x.
quiz.explain: This is sin[(π/3 + x) − x] = sin(π/3) = √3/2; the x cancels completely.
steps: Pattern: sin A cos B − cos A sin B = sin(A − B)
A = π/3 + x, B = x: A − B = π/3
quiz.mistake: Adds the angles instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Find cos 330°.
quiz.explain: cos(360° − 30°) = cos 30° = √3/2; cos is positive in quadrant IV.
steps: cos(2π − x) = cos x, so cos 330° = cos 30°
cos is positive in quadrant IV
quiz.mistake: Thinks every value in quadrant IV is negative

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): cos(−x) = cos x for every x.
Reason (R): Putting x = 0 in cos(x − y) gives cos(−y) = cos 0 cos y + sin 0 sin y = cos y.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and R actually derives A from the cos(x − y) formula.
steps: R: put x = 0 in cos(x − y): cos(−y) = cos 0 cos y + sin 0 sin y = 1·cos y + 0 = cos y
So R is true and gives cos(−y) = cos y for every y
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see that R is a proof of A

teach.ask: Gappu is lost in allied angles like cos(π − x) and sin(π/2 + x). Explain the cos(x + y) formula and a quick rule for allied angles.
teach.praise: π shifts keep the function, π/2 shifts swap it, and the quadrant gives the sign. I'm a pro now!
teach.nudge: When does sin turn into cos — with a π shift or a π/2 shift?

revise.summary: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y and cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y. From these come the allied-angle results for π/2 ± x, π ± x and 2π − x.
focus: State and use cos(x + y) and cos(x − y)
Simplify allied angles like π − x, π/2 + x and 2π − x with the correct sign
Find exact values such as cos 15°, cos 105° and cos 330°
Recognise expanded forms like cos A cos B + sin A sin B
remember: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y; cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y
cos(π/2 − x) = sin x, sin(π/2 − x) = cos x; cos(π/2 + x) = −sin x, sin(π/2 + x) = cos x
cos(π − x) = −cos x, sin(π − x) = sin x; cos(π + x) = −cos x, sin(π + x) = −sin x
cos(2π − x) = cos x, sin(2π − x) = −sin x
traps: In cos(x + y) the sign between the terms is '−', the opposite of the sign inside
cos(x + y) is not cos x + cos y

topics.title: sin(x ± y), tan(x ± y) and exact values

learn.hook: Your calculator knows sin 15°, but can you get its exact surd value with just 45° and 30°? Sum and difference formulas say yes.
points: sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y; sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y.
tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y), tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y), when the tangents and the result are defined.
cot(x + y) = (cot x cot y − 1)/(cot y + cot x); cot(x − y) = (cot x cot y + 1)/(cot y − cot x).
To prove an identity, expand the compound angles, use allied-angle values, and simplify one side to the other.

example.q: Find tan(π/4 + x) in terms of tan x.
steps: tan(π/4 + x) = (tan π/4 + tan x)/(1 − tan π/4 · tan x).

learn.reallife: Surveyors computing the height of a hill in the Western Ghats from two angles of elevation often combine angles with tan(x − y).

games.title: Match the expansion
pairs: sin x cos y + cos x sin y
sin x cos y − cos x sin y
(tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y)
(tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y)
(cot x cot y − 1)/(cot y + cot x)

quiz.q: sin(x − y) equals:
options: sin x cos y + cos x sin y
cos x cos y − sin x sin y
sin x cos y − cos x sin y
sin x sin y − cos x cos y
quiz.explain: For sine, the sign between the terms matches the sign inside the bracket.
steps: For sine, the sign between the terms matches the sign inside
'−' inside gives sin x cos y − cos x sin y
The '+' version is sin(x + y); the cos products belong to cos(x ± y)
sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y
Answer: sin x cos y − cos x sin y
quiz.mistake: Uses the cosine sign rule for sine

quiz.q: Find sin 40° cos 20° + cos 40° sin 20°.
steps: Pattern: sin A cos B + cos A sin B = sin(A + B)
quiz.mistake: Uses sin(40° − 20°)

quiz.q: If tan A = 1/2 and tan B = 1/3, then tan(A + B) is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets the denominator 1 − tan A tan B

quiz.q: tan(13π/12) equals:
quiz.explain: 13π/12 = π + π/12 and tan has period π, so tan(13π/12) = tan(π/12) = tan 15° = 2 − √3.
steps: tan has period π, so tan(13π/12) = tan(π/12) = tan 15°
quiz.mistake: Treats π + x like π − x and flips the sign

quiz.q: If tan x = 3 and tan y = 2, find tan(x − y).
steps: tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y)
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 − tan x tan y in the denominator

quiz.q: The value of sin 75° is:
steps: sin 75° = sin(45° + 30°) = sin 45° cos 30° + cos 45° sin 30°
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sin 75° with sin 15°

quiz.q: Simplify cos 4x cos x + sin 4x sin x.
quiz.explain: This is cos(4x − x) = cos 3x, using cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B.
steps: Pattern: cos A cos B + sin A sin B = cos(A − B)
quiz.mistake: Uses cos(A + B) and gets cos 5x

quiz.q: If sin A = 3/5 and cos B = 5/13, with A and B acute, find sin(A + B).
quiz.mistake: Uses sin(A − B) or cos(A + B)

teach.ask: Gappu wants sin 75° exactly, without a calculator. Explain the sin(x + y) and tan(x + y) formulas and use them.
teach.praise: 75° = 45° + 30°, and the formula does the rest. Exact and elegant!
teach.nudge: Which two familiar angles add up to 75°?

revise.summary: sin(x ± y) = sin x cos y ± cos x sin y, and tan(x ± y) = (tan x ± tan y)/(1 ∓ tan x tan y). They give exact values like sin 75° = (√6 + √2)/4 and tan 15° = 2 − √3.
focus: Expand sin(x ± y), tan(x ± y) and cot(x ± y)
Recognise expanded forms and fold them back into one angle
Find exact values of 15°, 75° and 105° type angles
Prove identities by expanding compound angles
remember: sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y; sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y
tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y); tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y)
traps: For sine the sign in the middle matches the sign inside; for cosine it is opposite
In tan(x − y), the denominator is 1 + tan x tan y, not 1 − tan x tan y

learn.hook: Put y = x in the sum formulas and you get the double-angle formulas — the most-used identities in Class 11 and 12 calculus.
points: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x = 2 tan x/(1 + tan²x).
cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x = (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x).
tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x).
sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x; cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x; tan 3x = (3 tan x − tan³x)/(1 − 3 tan²x).
Half angles: cos x = 2cos²(x/2) − 1 = 1 − 2sin²(x/2). Take the square root, then choose the sign from the quadrant of x/2.

example.q: If tan x = −3/4 and x lies in quadrant II, find sin(x/2), cos(x/2) and tan(x/2).
steps: x in quadrant II ⇒ π/2 < x < π ⇒ π/4 < x/2 < π/2, so all half-angle values are positive.

learn.reallife: The formula sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x tells a cricket coach that a ball thrown at 45° goes farthest (ignoring air resistance), because sin 90° = 1 is the largest.

games.title: Derive cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1
items: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y
Put y = x: cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x

quiz.q: If sin x = 3/5 and x is acute, then sin 2x is:
steps: x acute, sin x = 3/5 → cos x = √(1 − 9/25) = 4/5
quiz.mistake: Doubles sin x instead of using 2 sin x cos x

quiz.q: If cos x = 1/3, then cos 2x is:
quiz.mistake: Doubles cos x

quiz.q: If tan x = 1/2, then tan 2x is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets the denominator 1 − tan²x

quiz.q: cos 3x equals:
quiz.explain: cos 3x = 4cos³x − 3cos x; note the order is reversed compared with sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x.
steps: Triple angle for cosine: cos 3x = 4cos³x − 3cos x
The order is reversed compared with sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x
3 cos x − 4 cos³x is the wrong order
quiz.mistake: Copies the pattern of sin 3x

quiz.q: Using sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x, find sin 3x when sin x = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Cubes 1/2 as 1/6

quiz.q: If cos x = −1/3 and x lies in quadrant III, find sin(x/2).
steps: π < x < 3π/2 → π/2 < x/2 < 3π/4, quadrant II, so sin(x/2) > 0
quiz.mistake: Takes the sign from the quadrant of x instead of x/2

quiz.q: Which expression equals (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x)?
quiz.explain: Divide cos²x − sin²x by cos²x + sin²x = 1, then divide top and bottom by cos²x.
steps: cos 2x = (cos²x − sin²x)/(cos²x + sin²x), since the denominator is 1
Divide top and bottom by cos²x
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the tan 2x formula

quiz.q: Simplify 2 sin 15° cos 15°.
quiz.explain: 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x, so the value is sin 30° = 1/2.
steps: Formula: 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle twice to get sin 60°

teach.ask: Gappu forgot all three forms of cos 2x before the test. Explain how to get them from cos(x + y), and how to pick the sign for half angles.
teach.praise: One formula, three faces — and the half angle decides its own sign. Super!
teach.nudge: For sin(x/2), whose quadrant decides the sign: x or x/2?

revise.summary: Double-angle formulas: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x, cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x, tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x). Triple and half-angle results follow from them.
focus: Use all forms of sin 2x, cos 2x and tan 2x
Use sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x and cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x
Find half-angle values and choose the sign from the quadrant of x/2
Spot 2 sin x cos x as sin 2x in simplification
remember: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x = 2 tan x/(1 + tan²x)
cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x = (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x)
tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x)
sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x; cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x
traps: The order in cos 3x is reversed: 4 cos³x − 3 cos x, not 3 cos x − 4 cos³x
For half angles, the sign depends on the quadrant of x/2, not of x

learn.hook: When two tabla notes of nearly equal pitch play together, you hear 'beats'. The maths behind it is sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x+y)/2) cos((x−y)/2).
points: cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y); −2 sin x sin y = cos(x + y) − cos(x − y).
2 sin x cos y = sin(x + y) + sin(x − y); 2 cos x sin y = sin(x + y) − sin(x − y).
Proving identities: convert sums to products (or products to sums), cancel common factors, then use allied or double-angle results.
learn.reallife: Radio engineers mix two signals by multiplying them; the product-to-sum formula 2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y) shows the new frequencies that appear.

games.title: Spot the correct formula
items: 2 sin x cos y = sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)
Add the expansions of sin(x + y) and sin(x − y).
cos x − cos y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
There is a minus sign in front: −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
2 sin x sin y = cos(x − y) − cos(x + y)
This is −2 sin x sin y = cos(x + y) − cos(x − y) rearranged.

quiz.q: sin 5x + sin 3x equals:
quiz.explain: sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2) = 2 sin 4x cos x.
steps: Formula: sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2)
So sin 5x + sin 3x = 2 sin 4x cos x
quiz.mistake: Uses the pattern for sin A − sin B

quiz.q: cos 6x − cos 2x equals:
quiz.explain: cos A − cos B = −2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((A − B)/2) with A = 6x, B = 2x.
steps: Formula: cos A − cos B = −2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((A − B)/2)
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign

quiz.q: Find the exact value of cos 75° + cos 15°.
steps: cos A + cos B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2), with A = 75°, B = 15°
quiz.mistake: Adds cos 75° and cos 15° as cos 90°

quiz.q: 2 cos 45° cos 15° equals:
quiz.explain: 2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y) = cos 60° + cos 30°.
steps: Formula: 2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y)
quiz.mistake: Mixes up with the sin product formula

quiz.q: Find the value of sin 105° + cos 105°.
steps: So sin 105° + cos 105° = sin 105° − sin 15° = 2 cos 60° sin 45°
quiz.mistake: Thinks sin 105° and cos 105° cancel

quiz.q: Simplify (sin 5x − sin 3x)/(cos 5x + cos 3x).
quiz.explain: Numerator 2 cos 4x sin x, denominator 2 cos 4x cos x; the ratio is tan x.
steps: Numerator: sin 5x − sin 3x = 2 cos 4x sin x
Denominator: cos 5x + cos 3x = 2 cos 4x cos x
quiz.mistake: Cancels the wrong factor and keeps 4x

quiz.q: 2 sin 3x cos x equals:
quiz.explain: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B) = sin 4x + sin 2x.
steps: Formula: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B)
A = 3x, B = x: A + B = 4x, A − B = 2x
So 2 sin 3x cos x = sin 4x + sin 2x
quiz.mistake: Adds the angles without forming the sum and difference

quiz.q: Find the exact value of sin 75° − sin 15°.
steps: sin A − sin B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) sin((A − B)/2), with A = 75°, B = 15°
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°

teach.ask: Gappu needs to simplify (cos 9x + cos 3x)/(sin 9x − sin 3x). Explain the sum-to-product formulas and the half-sum, half-difference idea.

teach.nudge: When you add two cosines, which two new angles appear in the product?

revise.summary: Sum-to-product formulas turn sin x ± sin y and cos x ± cos y into products of half-sums and half-differences; product-to-sum formulas turn 2 sin x cos y and similar products into sums.
focus: Convert sums of sines and cosines into products
Convert products like 2 sin A cos B into sums
Find exact values such as cos 75° + cos 15° or sin 75° − sin 15°
Simplify quotients by cancelling common factors
remember: sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y); 2 sin x cos y = sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)

Use half-sums (x + y)/2 and half-differences (x − y)/2, not x + y and x − y
